position_in_era.historical_role: Mutation of the riff-first contract into a funk-groove sub-lineage: Joe Perry's staccato riff is derived from James Brown's rhythmic vocabulary rather than blues-based pentatonic descent. The riff's syncopation and call-and-response with the vocal established a funk-rock hybrid that directly spawned Run-DMC's 1986 collaboration — the first documented pathway from heavy metal riff culture into hip-hop. Leads the funk-groove sub-lineage that terminates in Killing in the Name.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded early 1975 at Record Plant, New York, produced by Jack Douglas. Perry's riff was inspired by a drum pattern he heard from the Muscle Shoals rhythm section — the riff is syncopated around the 'one' beat rather than landing on it, a James Brown principle applied to guitar. Tyler wrote the double-entendre lyric separately. The song was recorded at a medium tempo (122 bpm) that sits between rock and funk.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Perry (riff composer) and Tyler (vocal) are the primary pair. Tyler's vocal delivery mimics the riff's staccato rhythm — voice and riff share the same articulation pattern, an unusual alignment that makes the song feel like one unified percussive object rather than guitar plus vocal.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Perry: Gibson Les Paul; Tom Hamilton: bass following the riff with added syncopation; Brad Whitford: rhythm guitar; Joey Kramer: drums with a James Brown-influenced shuffle. The riff's staccato eighth-note pattern is distinct from Black Sabbath's legato power-chord sustain — speed and articulation carry the weight rather than register and sustain.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Original single reached #10 US (1977 re-release). The 1986 Run-DMC collaboration ('Walk This Way' featuring Tyler and Perry) reached #4 US and is considered the song that broke hip-hop into mainstream radio. The riff's funk DNA made the hip-hop translation natural rather than forced.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Toys in the Attic reached #11 US. The song was not initially a hit; its cultural significance grew through live performance and the eventual Run-DMC collaboration, which retroactively revealed the funk-groove pathway in the riff's DNA.
